title: Judge tosses DOJ case against ex-FBI officials accused of lying about Hunter Biden probe
description: Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism at the FBI Nikki Floris, testifies before the House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Wash
body: Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism at the FBI Nikki Floris, testifies before the House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, Oct. 22, 2019.Susan Walsh | APA federal judge on Monday blasted the Department of Justice for "weaponization" as he dismissed its case accusing two former FBI officials of lying to Congress about investigations into Hunter Biden, multiple news outlets reported.Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, in a hearing in U.S. District Court in Washington, reportedly tore into the DOJ over its "slapdash job" prosecuting ex-officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, saying he was "deeply troubled by what has happened here."Faruqui said the government lacked probable cause and failed to present evidence that the officials' statements before the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 were knowingly false, MS NOW reported. He also accused the DOJ of wrongly rushing the case ahead of the midterm election. The situation "cannot be described as anything other than weaponization," he said, according to MS NOW.The judge even apologized to the government's lawyers, calling it "incredibly unfair" that they were assigned to defend the flawed case."This does not feel like an investigation," Faruqui reportedly added. "It feels like a broken one-wish willow obsession."The DOJ, in response to an email sent to its press office, said it "disagrees" with the decision. "We are evaluating all options but cannot comment further on an ongoing criminal investigation," the agency said in response to CNBC. "The Department's actions will continue to be guided by the facts, the evidence, and the law – not politics."Attorneys for Floris and Benavides praised the judge's decision outside the courthouse later Monday morning."This case should never have been brought. The government had no case, as the judge just laid out," a lawyer for Floris said, slamming the prosecution as a "spaghetti-at-the-wall, Hunter-Biden-conspiracy fever dream."A lawyer for Benavides said they hope the DOJ will not try to keep the case alive by seeking an indictment before a grand jury "where they get to be behind closed doors and get to shape the narrative, and we are unable to present our side."The DOJ did not take that step when they unveiled the allegations against Floris and Benavides on Oct. 23. Rather, despite the alleged misconduct taking place years earlier, prosecutors acquired a criminal complaint, which only requires a judge's signature. Criminal complaints are often used to obtain arrest warrant in situations where prosecutors need to move quickly.Faruqui had flagged that circumstance as unusual, and last week refused to sign off on a superseding complaint that added an obstruction charge against the two ex-officials."I'm concerned with your view as to what the law is," the judge told the prosecutors in a hearing last Tuesday. "Why today, on this one case, have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?"

schema.headline: Judge tosses DOJ case against ex-FBI officials accused of lying about Hunter Biden probe

title: Social Security may have to cut retirement benefits in six years. Here's how much money is at stake for beneficiaries
description: Maryvit Luna - CNBC | Getty imagesSocial Security retirement benefits may face an automatic, across-the-board cut in just six years.Without interventi
body: Maryvit Luna - CNBC | Getty imagesSocial Security retirement benefits may face an automatic, across-the-board cut in just six years.Without intervention before then, the Social Security retirement trust fund, formally known as the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which helps pay benefits to eligible workers and qualifying family members, will run out in the fourth quarter of 2032, the program's trustees said in a June report.At that time, the trustees project retirement benefits will be cut by 22%.The Congressional Budget Office has a more dire forecast, anticipating that the retirement trust fund may run out sooner, in mid-2032, and that retirees may see larger benefit cuts, at 26%, upon insolvency. Beneficiaries may receive an average $500 cut to their monthly benefits across the U.S. based on a 24% benefit reduction, according to a June report from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. In 29 states, retirees would see even bigger average reductions, according to the nonpartisan organization focused on educating the public on fiscal policy issues. Senators elected this November will be in office in 2032, when the retirement trust fund depletion date hits. Their ability to right the ship is crucial for retirees and the economy. But it's not a sure thing given the political climate inside the beltway."The attention on 2032 is appropriate in the sense that that is when beneficiaries and future beneficiaries will see and feel the consequences of inaction," said Shai Akabas, vice president of economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a public policy think tank focused on promoting bipartisan cooperation."Nothing gets Congress to move like that type of deadline," he said.Of course, brinksmanship and political deadlock may stymie efforts. Congress could opt to kick the can down the road, rather than enact changes to shore up Social Security — which may require tax increases, benefit cuts or a combination of both.If lawmakers decide to combine Social Security's retirement and disability trust funds, the depletion date may move to the third quarter of 2034, when benefits may be cut by 17%, according to Social Security's trustees.Akabas said any delay by lawmakers would have consequences: Social Security's shortfall would continue to increase. There could also be consequences for the economy, he said.In 2023, Social Security benefits generated $2.6 trillion in total economic output and supported more than 12 million jobs, according to 2025 research by the National Institute on Retirement Security, a Washington, D.C., based nonprofit, nonpartisan organization.A 19% benefit cut could reduce gross domestic product by hundreds of billions of dollars, according to the NIRS research.Moreover, failing to muster Social Security reform would prompt bond market strain, according to research published in June by George Mason University's Mercatus Center. Social Security is tied to the bond market because its trust funds are invested in special issue U.S. Treasury bonds. If Social Security reform is delayed, that may put upward pressure on Treasury yields, with investors wanting higher returns for long-term bonds. Delayed reform may either prompt higher interest rates and borrowing costs or inflationary adjustments that hurt the value of government liabilities, according to the Mercatus Center research. Those changes may affect household budgets through higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and other types of consumer credit as well as student loans, according to the research. If interest rates and prices rise, that will interfere with economic growth, Akabas said."Those effects are also ones that the American people feel, in addition to adjustments to their benefits," Akabas said.Heading to the midterms, some Democratic congressional candidates have said they would raise or eliminate the Social Security payroll tax cap so high earners pay more into the program. In 2026, the 6.2% tax paid by both workers and their employers applies to earnings up to $184,500.Yet it remains to be seen whether Washington leaders will have the political will to address the problem soon. Tax increases, in particular, may not be viewed as politically popular heading into the 2028 presidential election.As such, payroll taxes are "extraordinarily unlikely" to rise in the next couple of years, said Jessica Riedl, a fellow at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center, which provides independent analyses of tax issues. If those tax hikes happen, it would likely be closer to 2032, she said."In Washington, they love to wait until the last minute," Riedl said. "There's no interest on either side for these sorts of tax increases in the short term. In the long term, I think everything is on the table."The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, founded by President Franklin D. Roosevelt's son, former U.S. Rep. James Roosevelt, has scored incumbent lawmakers on whether their votes have protected those programs.The advocacy organization has also endorsed candidates who support raising payroll taxes and protecting Social Security benefits from cuts. With those endorsements, the NCPSSM gives candidates a set of boxing gloves as a symbol of the fights they'll face in Congress, according to Dan Adcock, the NCPSSM's director of government relations and policy.The organization is also working to educate voters that the senators elected this year will be among those to deal with Social Security, he said."We've been trying to impress upon voters why this is an issue that should be top tier," Adcock said. "They need to be asking candidates about what their plans for the program would be."

schema.headline: Social Security may have to cut retirement benefits in six years. Here's how much money is at stake for beneficiaries

title: Anthropic reports $17 billion in Q3 revenue, purchase commitments of $895.4 billion in revised S-1
description: watch nowAnthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving inv
body: watch nowAnthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors a more comprehensive look into the state of its business. The artificial intelligence company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic had a loss of $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025.Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, bringing the company one step closer to a potentially historic initial public offering. The initial filing only included the Claude maker's financials through the first half of the year. During its third quarter, Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127% from the same period last year. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis, however. Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1.The company reported a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter. As the 5-year-old company prepares to kick off its roadshow, it will have to reckon with growing market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has been worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds, and quarterly reports from Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon last week added fuel to those concerns. The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows, causing some investors to worry that computing capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX, but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible.In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure." Anthropic said its compute and infrastructure expenses increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared with the same period last year. "As our compute and infrastructure capacity grows, the associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased," Anthropic said in the filing. The company's CEO, Dario Amodei, co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers who defected from OpenAI, now its chief rival. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the SEC in June, but its executives have signaled that it's aiming for a 2027 debut. Anthropic has worked to position itself as more safety-conscious than its competitors, and its S-1 includes more than 90 pages of risk factors. The company highlights risks, including potential political headwinds, its complex infrastructure needs as well as the difficulties that can come from balancing safety and commercial objectives."We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level," Anthropic's co-founders said in the filing.WATCH: Anthropic releases amended IPO prospectus with third-quarter financialswatch now

title: Australia hikes rates to 18-year high to fight inflation
description: Michele Bullock, governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), during a news conference at the central bank's head office in Sydney, Australia, on
body: Michele Bullock, governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), during a news conference at the central bank's head office in Sydney, Australia, on Tuesday, May 5, 2026. Australia's central bank raised its key interest rate for a third consecutive meeting, underscoring its determination to tame stubbornly strong inflation and cementing its outlier status among global counterparts. Photographer: Brendon Thorne/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesBloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAustralia's central bank raised its benchmark cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, the highest level since November 2008.The Reserve Bank of Australia's move was in line with expectations from economists polled by Reuters, and marked its fifth rate increase this year.In its statement, the RBA said that the move was a split decision, with six members voting for the increase and three opting for a hold. This also comes as the country continues to grapple with high inflation, with the consumer price index rising 4.3% in September, up from 4% in August and marking its highest level since March.The central bank also said inflation is now expected to "remain elevated through much of 2027," and not expected to fall back into its 2%-3% target range till late 2027, three quarters later than previously forecast. This was due to higher fuel and other commodity prices, in addition to factors including AI-related investment, which is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods, the RBA said.In its September decision, RBA governor Michelle Bullock said that inflation is "too high," driven by higher oil prices from the Iran War and stronger domestic spending. "We're seeing signs that upside risks to inflation are materializing," she added, saying that additional hikes will come "if that's what's needed to get inflation down."Growth has slowed in the first two quarters of 2026. Australia's GDP rose 2.1% in the June quarter compared to a year earlier, down from 2.5% in the March quarter.The RBA is trying to bring inflation back under control while higher borrowing costs and cost-of-living pressures weigh on households and activity. When asked if she sees a recession for Australia, Bullock said that it is "not our base case at the moment."

schema.headline: Australia hikes rates to 18-year high to fight inflation

title: Rubio says Trump wants to end Iran war 'peacefully' even as both sides prepare for strikes
description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during the Freedom 250 reception at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on October 20, 2026. Kylie Coop
body: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during the Freedom 250 reception at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on October 20, 2026. Kylie Cooper | Afp | Getty ImagesU.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force. Speaking over the weekend, Rubio told reporters that "He [Trump] hasn't made a decision...what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful. But we would prefer to do it peacefully."The remarks come as reports suggest both sides are gearing up for additional military strikes after the midterm elections. On Saturday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."He also ordered that its military database be updated so that "all kinds of physical and non-physical assets of the U.S.-Zionist enemy are brought within the reach of the Armed Forces," referring to U.S. and Israeli forces.Washington has not explicitly stated it plans to resume attacks on Iran, but reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. On Sunday, Trump told the Right Side Broadcasting Network. "We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other.""Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he added.Iran targets U.K. intelligenceOn Sunday, Iran's foreign ministry designated the U.K.'s Military Intelligence Services as a "hostile group" and accused the Royal Navy and Air Force of supporting "terrorist organizations."In a Telegram post, the ministry said that the move was a response to what it called London's "malicious" actions, including the designation of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a "terrorist organization."Tehran has separately accused the U.K. of participating in the U.S.-Iran war by allowing American forces access to British military and logistical bases.The U.K. had allowed U.S. forces to use RAF Fairford and Diego Garcia for what were described as "defensive" strikes on Iran, according to the BBC.

schema.headline: Rubio says Trump wants to end Iran war 'peacefully' even as both sides prepare for strikes

title: OpenAI hires former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for national security role
description: WEST POINT, NEW YORK - MAY 23: Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll arrives for the United States Military Academy commencement ceremony in Michie Stadi
body: WEST POINT, NEW YORK - MAY 23: Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll arrives for the United States Military Academy commencement ceremony in Michie Stadium at the U.S. Military Academy on May 23, 2026 in West Point, New York. U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth was announced as the 2026 commencement speaker just two days before the event. (Photo by Adam Gray/Getty Images)Adam Gray | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesOpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company. Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position. He will work with OpenAI's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular focus on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly.OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the U.S. has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology."National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said. He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security. I'm joining OpenAI to help the U.S. and our allies put this technology to work responsibly, for the people who keep us safe.Dan DriscollSenior Counselor, OpenAIThe appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S. Army announcement.Driscoll also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from the Presidential Office of Ukraine. At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's efforts to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services through its Daybreak program.

schema.headline: OpenAI hires former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for national security role

title: Prediction market traders now see nearly 75% chance of Democrats winning the Senate
description: A Kalshi billboard displaying US Senate midterm election odds in New York, US, on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMoment
body: A Kalshi billboard displaying US Senate midterm election odds in New York, US, on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMomentum for Democrats is building on Kalshi, with traders on Monday seeing a 74% chance of the party winning control of the U.S. Senate — the highest odds seen for the party on the platform since the market first opened. The higher odds come after The New York Times reported Sunday that a poll it conducted with Siena University found Democrats are leading in several battleground states, strengthening Democrats' path to a possible Senate majority. The contract asks "Who will control the Senate?" and will be verified by the Library of Congress after Tuesday's vote. Since it opened in 2024, Republicans dominated the market for Senate control in 2026. The gap between the parties' odds narrowed shortly after the U.S. and Israel first launched strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, though the chances for Republican control jumped up to 60% in July before reversing in mid-September. Markets on separate Senate races have also seen major movement in favor of Democratic candidates in the last 24 hours. Traders on Kalshi now see a 74% chance of Democrats winning the Senate race in Texas, up from 68.4%, over the past 24 hours. The market on the Senate race in Iowa jumped to 50% from 42% on Polymarket in favor of Democrats. In Kansas, which has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1932, odds of Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton winning over Republican Roger Marshall are up to 63% from 52%.Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Prediction market traders now see nearly 75% chance of Democrats winning the Senate

title: Canada-India $5.5 billion bank takeover attracts opposition from workers, politicians
description: GERMANY - 2026/05/20: In this photo illustration, the logo of company Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited is displayed on a smartphone in front of abst
body: GERMANY - 2026/05/20: In this photo illustration, the logo of company Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited is displayed on a smartphone in front of abstract background on computer screen. Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesCanadian firm Fairfax Financial Holdings' proposed $5.5 billion takeover of IDBI Bank is facing pushback from employees of the Indian state-owned lender and political parties in the country.On Sunday, the United Forum of IDBI Officers and Employees called for a two-day "nationwide" strike against the sale of the bank to Fairfax. The workers' union also expressed "grave concerns" about the transparency of the sale and valuation process, according to a post on X. It is demanding that the government "cancel the privatization process" and instead focus on strengthening the bank while protecting public investment and employees' interests. Last week, Rahul Gandhi, India's leader of the opposition, extended support to the IDBI Bank employee unions opposing the takeover by Fairfax. "Public banks are not assets to be sold off, they are tools to build the nation," Gandhi said in a statement on Thursday. He added that the sale of over 60% stake in IDBI Bank to Fairfax goes against the commitment of previous governments to hold a 51% stake in the state-owned lender.Nirmala Sitharaman, India's finance minister, in her response said the public sector bank was handed to the government in "poor shape" and was revived through "professionalism, prudence" and recapitalization of more than 250 billion rupees ($2.6 billion)."The IDBI Bank is now poised for its next phase of growth," the finance minister said. The government has previously said that the next phase of growth will be driven by a strategic investor.The Indian government on Oct.14 said the sale of over 60% of the share in IDBI will mark the largest foreign direct investment transaction in India's financial sector. Fairfax made a bid to pay 81 rupees per share for IDBI against the average fair value set at 75.99 rupees apiece.On Monday, shares of IDBI opened at around 79 rupees per share.However, Indian media outlet Businessworld on Thursday reported that government officials had suppressed the valuation of IDBI to make Fairfax's offer seem attractive. The Ministry of Finance has defended its procedure, adding that the bidding process was a "double blind" as the bidder did not know the valuation and the valuators did not see the bids.The Indian government has been divesting stakes this year as it pushes to keep the country's growth engine running amid deepening fiscal pressures. It sold shares in several companies, including Cochin Shipyard, Indian Railways Finance Corp, NHPC and Coal India. In August, it got $3.3 billion for a 6.5% stake in the country's top life insurer, Life Insurance Corporation of India.

schema.headline: Canada-India $5.5 billion bank takeover attracts opposition from workers, politicians

title: U.S. reportedly strikes Iran's Qeshm Island as Vance hopes for ‘negotiated settlement’ with Tehran
description: JOINT BASE ANDREWS, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 2: Vice President JD Vance descends from Air Force Two on November 2, 2026 in Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. Th
body: JOINT BASE ANDREWS, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 2: Vice President JD Vance descends from Air Force Two on November 2, 2026 in Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. The Vice President returned to Washington following midterm campaign stops in New York and Ohio. Tom Brenner | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesThe U.S. reportedly carried out strikes against Iran on Monday even as Vice President JD Vance expressed hopes of reaching a "negotiated settlement" with Tehran.America attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, which added that Washington has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks. The military campaign against Iran has been kept quiet on purpose so as not to signal any intention of major combat escalation, the report said, quoting an unnamed official.Qeshm Island, off Iran's southern coast, is the largest island in the Persian Gulf. Located near the Strait of Hormuz, it has emerged as a potential U.S. target amid reports that anti-ship missiles, mines, drones and attack craft are being kept there in underground tunnels.President Donald Trump's administration has been talking down risks of an all-out war with Iran, with Vance being the latest to claim "good progress" in talks with Iran."The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement," Vance told CNN on Monday. He added, though, that Iranians are "unpredictable" and Trump retains "kinetic and non-kinetic" options against Tehran. Vance said that Washington has not set any deadline for reaching a peace deal with Iran.Nuclear threatTrump said earlier Monday that the U.S. had to go to war with Iran to stop the country from having "a nuclear weapon," that "we're not going to allow Iran ever to have a nuclear weapon. And they understand that."Last month, the president had said the U.S. will not attack Iran before the midterm elections, after polls ahead of the ballot showed that support for the war had dwindled, with only 31% of Americans supporting the military action.  Trump told Fox News in an interview Monday night that the U.S. had to take a "little detour" to Iran to stop the country from having nuclear weapons. The president said that the U.S. has bombed out all of Iran's potential nuclear power, but he might target Pickaxe Mountain next. Located south of Iran's Natanz enrichment plant, Pickaxe Mountain houses an underground nuclear facility. "We might have to go after Pickaxe, but that's not a big deal," Trump said, adding the U.S. could destroy it in one hour.On Nov. 1, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio had also said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.

schema.headline: U.S. reportedly strikes Iran's Qeshm Island as Vance hopes for ‘negotiated settlement’ with Tehran

title: Crude oil prices sell off more than 7% on Iran peace talk hopes ahead of U.S. midterms
description: watch nowCrude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signalled they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict
body: watch nowCrude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signalled they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures shed 7.4% to close at $96.46 a barrel, the biggest daily loss since July 27. Brent crude, the international benchmark, lost 7.6% to settle at $104.77 a barrel. President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that Iran wants to "make a deal and that could happen." U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend that Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections, gaining more than 10% in October. The oil market has sold off during previous phases of the war on rumors of a possible settlement, only for the conflict to subsequently escalate and spike prices again.Stock Chart IconStock chart icon Brent Trump "hasn't made a decision" on whether to strike Iran again, Rubio told reporters. "What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully." Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency. Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the government certain authorities to do this, Pezeshkian said.Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to IRNA.Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said. Stock Chart IconStock chart icon wtiBut Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities. "With that said, so long as there is no concrete conclusion to the war, and tanker and Houthi attacks remain prevalent, we do not anticipate a complete erosion of the risk premium via diplomacy headlines alone," McKay said. — CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Crude oil prices sell off more than 7% on Iran peace talk hopes ahead of U.S. midterms

title: Palantir reports booming U.S. commercial revenue growth, topping government for first time
description: watch nowPalantir beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates after the bell on Monday, with U.S. commercial revenue topping government for the first t
body: watch nowPalantir beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates after the bell on Monday, with U.S. commercial revenue topping government for the first time as businesses adopt more of the company's artificial intelligence tools.Shares dipped about 3% in extended trading.Here's how the company did compared to LSEG estimates:Earnings per share: 44 cents adjusted vs. 41 cents expected Revenue: $2.31 billion vs. $2.18 billion expectedRevenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time ever, Palantir said. Net income more than doubled to $1.13 billion, or 44 cents per share, from about $476 million, or 18 cents per share."I don't believe anyone's had consistent results like this in the history of software AI, ever," CEO Alex Karp told CNBC's Seema Mody in an interview, adding that the business is succeeding without salespeople.Palantir has long been known for its strength in the government sector, but its commercial segment caught up in Q3.U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, surpassing U.S. government revenue of $953 million, which was up 96%. The company's U.S. commercial revenue has more than quintupled over the last two years.Palantir lifted its guidance, saying it now expects U.S. commercial revenue "in excess of" $3.56 billion for the full year. Last quarter, the company boosted its forecast to $3.42 billion. The company projects about $2.65 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and about $8.53 billion for full-year 2026.Karp has openly supported the use of open-weight models and criticized leading AI labs, which he told CNBC earlier this year are forcing businesses to sell their data sovereignty. Karp, on Monday, also reiterated recent calls to nationalize AI labs, calling it the "only realistic way" to manage liability.In September, Karp joined major tech CEOs at the White House as calls for regulation mounted following claims from AI researchers that the technology has a more than 10% of killing humanity."My message to everybody is: Beware of thinking you can delay the future in AI," he told CNBC. "The future is here. The political ramifications of it are here."Stock Chart IconStock chart iconPalantir stock chart.Read more CNBC tech newsHumans are still doing the work behind some AI agentsOpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest roundBinance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion hack, says 90% of stolen user assets are coveredWhy AI is boosting Meta’s ad business while hurting Google search

title: Lumentum CEO touts 'enormous' opportunity in massive AI connectivity deal with Marvell
description: watch nowMarvell Technology's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands
body: watch nowMarvell Technology's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday."You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here."Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release.Marvell shares slumped 13% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank nearly 19%. But both stocks have been huge winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with Marvell more than doubling in the past year, prior to Monday's sell-off, and Lumentum quadrupling over that stretch. Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models."We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said. Read more CNBC tech newsHumans are still doing the work behind some AI agentsOpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest roundBinance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion hack, says 90% of stolen user assets are coveredWhy AI is boosting Meta’s ad business while hurting Google searchLumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028.Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology.Marvell's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies. In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers. "This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them."Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone.watch nowCORRECTION: This story has been updated to reflect that Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston described the deal as an 'enormous' opportunity. A previous version of this story incorrectly cited the Marvell CEO.

schema.headline: Lumentum CEO touts 'enormous' opportunity in massive AI connectivity deal with Marvell

title: I bonds now pay 5.51% — but there are trade-offs. What to know before buying
description: dowell | Moment | Getty ImagesNow that Series I bonds pay higher interest, the government-backed, nearly risk-free asset could be more attractive for
body: dowell | Moment | Getty ImagesNow that Series I bonds pay higher interest, the government-backed, nearly risk-free asset could be more attractive for certain investors. But I bonds have downsides, and there are alternatives to consider. Newly purchased I bonds currently pay 5.51% annual interest through April 30, up from the 4.26% yield offered on purchases made through October. Amid rising inflation, the variable part of I bond interest rose to 4.08%, while the fixed part increased to 1.40%, the highest since 2006. Combined, the 5.51% composite rate is the biggest yield since November 2022.The new I bond rate is "very attractive," according to Ken Tumin, founder of DepositQuest.com, a blog that tracks I bond rates, among other deposit accounts.The variable part of I bond interest resets every six months, based on the consumer price index. For the next six months after purchase, I bonds look "very competitive" compared to other shorter-term options for cash, such as savings accounts or certificates of deposit, according to Tumin. Read more CNBC personal finance coverageMidterm election: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisionsThese Senate races may help determine the fate of Social SecuritySocial Security: How much money beneficiaries may lose if Congress does nothingTrump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in DecemberCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026Meanwhile, the I bond's 1.4% fixed rate stays the same for as long as you own it, which could appeal to longer-term investors, he said.But I bonds aren't right for everyone. Here are some key things to know before purchasing.I bonds can be a 'secondary emergency fund'Investors can buy $10,000 of electronic I bonds per person per calendar year via their TreasuryDirect account. You can open additional TreasuryDirect accounts for other family members or businesses to buy more. I bond interest is tax-deferred until redemption and is not subject to state or local taxes. You can also avoid federal taxes if you use the money for qualified education expenses.But experts say there are some downsides. The funds are locked up for 12 months from purchase, and you'll lose your last three months of interest if you redeem within five years.Advisors typically recommend keeping at least three to six months of living expenses in cash for emergency savings. I bonds could boost those reserves, experts say, as long as you keep enough readily accessible cash elsewhere."I always say [I bonds are] a secondary emergency fund," said David Enna, founder of Tipswatch.com, a website that tracks Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, and I bond rates.Once you own I bonds for five years, you can redeem the money as needed, penalty-free. I bond alternativesWith I bond purchase limits, restrictions and some TreasuryDirect complaints, advisors often recommend other options for clients who want to preserve purchasing power."For most of my clients, I bonds are more hassle than they're worth," said certified financial planner Eileen Olson, founder of advisory firm Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina. "The amount is too small to matter."On a $2 million portfolio, the $10,000 annual purchase limit is only 0.5%, and it earns about $550 in a year before federal taxes, she said. "That won't protect anyone's lifestyle from inflation."Instead, Olson prefers TIPS, which don't have purchase limits and can be bought alongside other assets, outside TreasuryDirect. TIPS have five-, 10- and 30-year terms, with yields ranging from about 2.3% to above 3% for the 30-year term, as of Nov. 2. watch nowHowever, the right option depends on your investing goals and timeline, experts say."For short-term cash, Treasury bills and high-yield savings are simpler," Olson said.Also backed by the U.S. government, Treasury bills, or T-bills, have terms ranging from four weeks up to 52 weeks. As of Nov. 2, some T-bill yields were well over 4%. By comparison, the top 1% average of high-yield savings accounts were paying above 4%, according to rate comparison site DepositAccounts. Some one-year certificates of deposit were also offering rates over 4%, the same day, according to Bankrate. Money market funds are another option. Some of the biggest funds were paying around 4%, as of Nov. 2, according to Crane Data.

title: North Korea denies links to Binance hack as researchers trace stolen billions
description: Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.Jorge Silva | ReutersNorth Korea rejected U.S. allegations linking Pyongyang to the estimated
body: Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.Jorge Silva | ReutersNorth Korea rejected U.S. allegations linking Pyongyang to the estimated $6.3 billion Binance hack, calling the accusation a “grave political provocation,” according to state media.Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, denounced the FBI's attribution of the attack to North Korea-linked hacking group TraderTraitor, Yohnap reported Tuesday, citing the state-run Korean Central News Agency."The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state', claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," Kim said, according to KCNA.She accused Washington of misleading international public opinion by portraying cybercrimes around the world as the work of North Korea.Separately, Binance said Tuesday it would begin progressively reopening withdrawals for additional crypto assets across more networks, expanding its phased restoration of services following last week's  hack. The denial comes as blockchain analytics firms trace billions of dollars in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance through thousands of wallets across multiple blockchains.Elliptic and Chainalysis said hackers linked to North Korea have used increasingly complex techniques to obscure the trail of the funds.In the first four days after the attack, the hackers used roughly 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains and conducted more than 40,000 transactions, Elliptic said in a report Monday. The activity appeared highly complex and automated, with an average of one new wallet used every 25 seconds.Much of the laundering activity initially took place on the Tron blockchain, where stolen funds were distributed across about 7,700 addresses before being moved to Ethereum through cross-chain bridges, according to Elliptic. At least $147 million had been transferred out of Tron through such bridges.The hackers also used decentralized exchanges to swap stolen stablecoins into cryptocurrencies that cannot be frozen by their issuers, including ether. Elliptic said roughly $786 million in stablecoins was converted before issuers including Tether and Circle froze the remaining assets.The laundering operation has since expanded to other blockchains, including Solana. Chainalysis said North Korea-linked actors had begun a new phase of laundering after moving more than $500 million through intermediary wallets on Tron.Elliptic also identified the first signs of bitcoin mixing, a technique designed to make transactions harder to trace. About 28 bitcoin, worth $2.2 million, had passed through 18 mixing transactions as of early Monday, the firm said.Despite the extensive movement of funds, about $2.85 billion — or 44% of exactly $6.43 billion stolen as reported by Elliptic — has been frozen or seized, while roughly $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, mostly in bitcoin and ether.The firm said only a negligible amount of stolen funds appeared to have been cashed out, with most of the activity involving transfers or conversions between cryptocurrencies rather than exchanges into spendable funds.Elliptic said the laundering has moved slower than after the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, when North Korean hackers moved all the stolen ether within 10 days. It expects the remaining funds to be gradually converted into bitcoin and potentially cashed out through over-the-counter brokers and exchanges over several months.Binance added it has covered about 95% of the affected amount, with the remaining 5% consisting of less liquid tokens that take longer to source. The exchange said it was working with industry partners to acquire the remaining assets.

schema.headline: North Korea denies links to Binance hack as researchers trace stolen billions

title: Trump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in December
description: SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell celebrates with family and other SpaceX employees at the Nasdaq Marketsite in New York af
body: SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell celebrates with family and other SpaceX employees at the Nasdaq Marketsite in New York after the SpaceX initial public offering on June 12, 2026.Spencer Platt | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesEligible Trump Account holders will begin receiving donated shares of SpaceX stock next month, according to an X post on Friday."Robert and I are thrilled that our gift of over 2 million shares of SpaceX stock will be distributed to children's Trump accounts in December!" President and COO Gwynne Shotwell wrote in the post. The gift from Shotwell and her husband will provide a share apiece to around 2 million Trump Accounts holders ages 11 to 17 who live in ZIP codes with median family incomes of $57,000 or less, or in ZIP codes with too few residents for a median family income to be reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. These families should receive a notice by Monday, Shotwell wrote on X. "In a few weeks, an additional gift will be finalized for eligible 11 to 17-year-old children in military families serving overseas, children in foster care, and more children whose MFI is $90,000 or less living in counties near our home in the great state of Texas," she also wrote. Parents or guardians can check eligibility for the donation through Invest America, a nonprofit advocacy group, and track account activity with the Trump Accounts app.Read more CNBC personal finance coverageMidterm election: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisionsThese Senate races may help determine the fate of Social SecuritySocial Security: How much money beneficiaries may lose if Congress does nothingTrump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in DecemberCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts, are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.Children born from 2025 through 2028 may also receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria. In a separate funding announcement in October, Elon Musk wrote in an X post that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX sometime in 2027, which may also come via Trump Accounts. The U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold donated individual stocks, a change from previous guidelines that only allowed diversified, low-cost index funds.The move to permit stock donations could pave the way for more large-scale philanthropic gifts, Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Oct. 8. On Oct. 29, Bisignano announced his own donation to Trump Accounts for eligible children ages 2 to 8 living in 11234, Bisignano's hometown ZIP code, according to The Bisignano Family Fund.

schema.headline: Trump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in December
